summary: Source-anchored research for Synthetic-chart signals with real-price execution. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: QuantConnect documents that its RenkoConsolidator can emit multiple fixed-size bricks in one time step when a single tick jumps across several thresholds. Methodological implication: emitted bricks must retain their actual availability time; their intermediate levels must not automatically become sequential executable fills. (medium confidence)

TradingView warns that Renko brick levels can be disconnected from actual market prices at a given moment. Its synthetic-chart backtest fills therefore cannot be treated as contemporaneous real-price executions. (low confidence)

Heikin-Ashi OHLC values average current and previous price information and are synthetic rather than executable market prices. Schwab independently warns that the displayed price may differ from the actual trading price and that signals can arrive later than on ordinary candles. (medium confidence)

TradingView warns that default strategy fills on non-standard charts use the chart’s synthetic OHLC. For Renko, brick levels can be disconnected from market prices, and historical box formation can differ from realtime formation. These backtests do not establish achievable executions. (medium confidence)

QuantConnect distinguishes range bars from Renko: a range bar fixes the whole bar’s high-minus-low span, while its described Renko construction uses fixed price movement from the opening price. Range-bar formation depends on price movement rather than a fixed elapsed-time interval. This describes QuantConnect’s documented construction, not every platform’s range-bar implementation. (low confidence)

A causal evaluation should distinguish signal availability, order submission, and actual fill records rather than assign a fill to the synthetic signal price. This is a methodological inference from TradingView’s documented historical-after-close/realtime-after-new-tick emulator behavior and PineConnector’s explicit separation of strategy rule, chart price, and broker execution. (medium confidence)

The negation check scopes the failure claim rather than banning synthetic signals. Melki argues that tick-resolution data, consistent Renko construction, fixed brick size, visible wicks, and appropriate entry/exit processing can permit a reliable Renko backtest. This is his conditional methodological position, not a validated guarantee for TradingView or SOL/Jupiter execution. (low confidence)

Heikin-Ashi OHLC values are synthetic averages rather than actual market prices. Schwab independently warns that the displayed current price may differ from the actual trading price. A signal derived from those values does not establish an executable entry price. (high confidence)

QuantConnect defines a range bar by the whole bar high-minus-low range rather than fixed elapsed time. Its bar-completion rule follows price movement; an equally spaced bar index is not evidence of equally spaced decision times. The second sentence is a methodological inference. (low confidence)

For its documented chart-timeframe crossover example, TradingView avoids intrabar repainting by requiring execution on the final bar iteration, when prices are confirmed. Methodological implication: a backtest that uses the finished synthetic bar must date that decision at confirmation rather than earlier within the bar. This does not establish that every requested data context is confirmed. (low confidence)

TradingView’s June 2023 announcement introduced standard-OHLC simulated fills for Heikin-Ashi. Its help center explains that each ordinary time bar has exactly one Heikin-Ashi bar, allowing synthetic-data calculations with ordinary-price entry and exit simulation. The announcement explicitly excludes Renko from this fill-setting change. (medium confidence)

An implementation pattern is to run the strategy on standard candles and request Heikin-Ashi data only for signal conditions. TradingView documents ticker.heikinashi() with request.security() on any chart type; a Stack Overflow answer independently recommends this standard-chart architecture for Heikin-Ashi backtesting. (medium confidence)

In his Renko backtesting article, Benjamin Melki describes a next-bar-open bias: a forming continuation brick can vanish after reversal, so a live entry based on that forming brick may disappear from the historical chart. He also explains that constructing Renko from time bars loses the intrabar tick path. These are described mechanisms, not a measured crypto loss estimate. (low confidence)

TradingView documents that realtime high, low and close remain fluid until bar close, while historical OHLC lacks intermediate movements. Its same-timeframe example waits for barstate.isconfirmed to suppress an intrabar cross that may disappear. PineConnector separately stresses that waiting for confirmation and using realistic execution prices address different problems. (medium confidence)

For higher-timeframe requests, TradingView documents requesting the previous confirmed value with a one-bar expression offset and barmerge.lookahead_on; its example uses close[1]. This specific pattern concerns higher-timeframe confirmation. It does not establish that a synthetic brick’s historical price was executable at the signal time. (low confidence)

TradingView’s broker emulator infers intrabar paths from OHLC by default, with different assumed high/low orderings according to the opening price. Methodological implication: replacing synthetic prices with ordinary OHLC still leaves intrabar execution assumptions; it does not recover the observed tick sequence. (medium confidence)

A Sierra Chart support thread reports a Renko bar-based backtest whose timed flattening occurred late; the reporter later said correcting use of sc.BaseDataEndDateTime resolved the timing issue. This is a user-reported timestamp-handling case, not evidence of a platform-wide defect or a crypto incident. (low confidence)

TradingView’s documentation uses different wording about Heikin-Ashi suitability: the non-standard-data page calls synthetic HA prices unsuited to backtesting or automated trading, while the help center permits HA calculations with standard-chart entry and exit prices. These attributed statements distinguish the price representation from a supported simulation configuration; neither demonstrates live fill equivalence. (low confidence)

TradingView documents a scoped exception: its standard-OHLC fill option lets a strategy evaluated on Heikin-Ashi data use actual market prices for simulated fills. Its June 2023 announcement explicitly says Renko backtests still use synthetic prices. This is a simulation feature, not a broker execution guarantee. (low confidence)

TradingView documents next-available-tick fills as its broker emulator default. Using a real-price series does not by itself justify assigning an immediate fill at a synthetic signal price; order creation and eligible fill time remain separate events. The second sentence is a methodological inference. (low confidence)

TradingView identifies future data leaking into past evaluation as lookahead bias. Real-price fill assumptions alone do not prove causal signal construction; the information used to decide must also have been available at the recorded decision time. The second sentence is a methodological inference. (low confidence)
